The length of the normal menstrual cycle varies from woman to woman, the average is 28 days, and 22 to 35 days are within the normal range.

The stages of the female menstrual cycle can usually be divided into two dimensions: the ovarian cycle and the uterine cycle. The stages of the ovarian cycle can be divided into the follicular phase, the day of ovulation, and the luteal phase. The stages of the uterine cycle can be divided into menstrual period, growth period, ovulation day and secretion period. (Note: ovulation is not a stage, but a dividing line)

Generally speaking, the period from the onset of menstrual cramps to the day of ovulation is the follicular phase. The menstrual period belongs to the early follicular phase in the follicular phase. During the menstrual period, small follicles have begun to develop. After the menstrual period is over, it belongs to the real follicular phase. During this period, the granulosa cells of the follicle produce estrogen. Under the action of estrogen, the endometrium rapidly proliferates, blood vessels proliferate, and the glands widen and lengthen, but do not secrete. At the end of this period, the ovaries ovulate. 

The day of ovulation is the day when the eggs are released; in the case of normal menstruation, ovulation is counted from the first day of the next menstrual period, and the ovulation day is usually counted down 12 to 16 days; Measures the period when the case is most likely to conceive. The luteal phase runs from ovulation to the day before the next menstrual cramp. During the luteal phase, the ovaries are affected by hormones and secrete progesterone to maintain the thickened endometrium to facilitate the implantation of the fertilized egg. Menstruation again marks the end of the current menstrual cycle and the beginning of a new menstrual cycle.

2. How to have enough deep sleep?

According to the American College of Physicians (ACP) guidelines for the management of chronic insomnia disorders in adults, cognitive and behavioral therapy is recommended as the initial treatment of insomnia. Clinical practice shows that people with chronic insomnia usually have some bad sleep habits. If you want to improve sleep quality and alleviate the situation of excessive light sleep and insufficient deep sleep, you can refer to the following sleep improvement suggestions:
 (1) Psychological factors: Excessive excitement, anxiety, mental tension, depression and other emotions may lead to increased light sleep and insufficient deep sleep. Generally, with the relief of these emotional reactions, sleep quality can be improved. 
 (2) Physiological factors: Excessive fatigue and physical discomfort caused by various diseases (such as pain, itching, cough, etc.) may lead to excessive light sleep and insufficient deep sleep. 
 (3) Environmental factors: light, noise, temperature and humidity and other factors will interfere with sleep, keep a quiet, comfortable and dark bedroom environment, choose suitable bedding, pillows and mattresses, which will help to improve excessive light sleep and deep sleep. Insufficient sleep. 
 (4) Life rhythm: Shift work, jet lag, irregular work and rest and other factors will disrupt the body's biological clock, resulting in too much light sleep and insufficient deep sleep. Taking regular breaks, going to bed on time, getting up on time to meet the sun, and allowing the biological clock to function properly can improve sleep quality. 
 (5) Diet: Caffeine, nicotine, alcohol and stimulating food all interfere with deep sleep, resulting in excessive light sleep. Stay away from tobacco and alcohol, avoid coffee, strong tea, and dinner to avoid overeating. 
 (6) Exercise: When exercising properly to increase physical fatigue, the human body needs to increase the time of deep sleep to eliminate fatigue, and the proportion of light sleep will decrease accordingly. However, strenuous exercise should be avoided right before bed, as the arousal and high body temperature may make it difficult for you to fall asleep.

In light sleep, the electrical activity of the brain slows down, the heart rate and breathing rate slow down, and the person falls asleep but is easily awakened. Waking up from sleep is a protective mechanism and a necessity for health and survival, so light sleep is also a normal physiological need. However, if the proportion of light sleep in the total sleep time is too high, the quality of sleep will deteriorate, and it is easy to feel that you cannot wake up and cannot relieve fatigue.
2. How to improve the situation of excessive light sleep?

The causes of awakenings during nighttime sleep are complex, ranging from short-lived micro-awakens to long-lasting awakenings. Humans are not necessarily aware of all arousal, and the state of not awake may be related to a variety of factors, such as sleep disturbances, sleeping too little or too much. Under normal circumstances, the number of awakenings during the night is less than 2, and the total awakening time does not exceed 10% of the total sleep time. If you wake up frequently at night, you may be insomniacs with difficulty in maintaining sleep. The proportion of deep sleep in this group is usually significantly lower than that of the normal population. Even if the total sleep time does not decrease, there will be poor physical recovery after waking up.

Sleep is divided into rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and non–rapid eye movement (Mon–REM, NREM) sleep, of which NREM sleep includes light sleep and deep sleep. During sleep, REM sleep alternates with NREM sleep, each time being called a sleep cycle. A normal person\'s whole night\'s sleep generally contains 4–6 sleep cycles, one cycle is about 90–100 minutes, and each cycle is not a simple repetition of the previous cycle. Generally, in later sleep cycles, REM sleep time increases and NREM sleep time decreases. A typical sleep rhythm is state transitions in the following order: wake-light sleep-deep sleep-light sleep-rapid eye movement. However, in the actual sleep process, not all sleep states are necessarily experienced, and the transitions between sleep states are not necessarily completely regular. For example, a person can go directly from any one of light sleep, deep sleep and REbM to wakefulness.

During deep sleep, the frequency of brain waves is significantly slower, and the breathing rate and blood pressure are also significantly reduced, so deep sleep is also called slow-wave sleep. In the deep sleep stage, the sleep program is the deepest and the wake-up threshold is the highest. If awakened during deep sleep, symptoms such as dizziness, palpitations, and irritability may occur. Studies have found that in the deep sleep stage, the brain can be fully rested, and the effect of eliminating fatigue is also the best. Deep sleep is extremely important for stabilizing emotions, balancing mentality, and restoring energy. Generally speaking, the longer the deep sleep time, the better the sleep quality. However, the long-term high proportion of deep sleep may be a signal of the onset of certain diseases, and it is recommended to seek the guidance of a professional doctor.
